clue.text: Makes special parts from spare plastic?

definitions.text: Makes special parts from spare plastic?

blocks.clueFragment: Makes special parts from spare plastic?
blocks.note: surface reading: a factory turning waste plastic into bespoke components
setter's reading: 'spare' made plastic, so its letters reshaped, gives words like PARSE, SPEAR and PEARS, each one a rearranged word

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'plastic' as mouldable: remould the letters of 'spare' and you get new words. The things you make that way are the crossword device itself, and 'parts' nearly is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearranging the letters of one word to form another produces these, so the whole clue describes making them.

clue.text: Incompetent A-lister?

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: lacking the skill, not up to it
second meaning: a celebrity, a person of note

explanation.walkthrough: The answer split in two reads NOT ABLE, which is incompetent; kept whole it is a noun for a famous person.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a prominent person, and an A-lister is a top-tier celebrity, so the noun fits the second meaning.

clue.text: Green jumper made from recycled rags by customer

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and made into something new, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
a customer is someone who shops

explanation.surface: An eco-friendly green sweater knitted from recycled rags, bought by a customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green jumper' wants to be a sweater, since jumper is British for a pullover; here it is a green insect that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect is typically green and moves by leaping, so it is literally a green thing that jumps.

clue.text: House is different when the front is removed

indicators.note: removing the front means the opening letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: something that is different from before has changed

explanation.surface: Someone notices a house looks different once its front has been taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: House here is astrological: the zodiac has twelve houses, and the first is the Ram.
explanation.definitionFit: In astrology the twelve signs are also called houses, and the Ram is the first of them.

clue.text: Fruit positioned alongside poison shrub, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is lost

blocks.note: something positioned has been sat in place
poison sumac is a toxic North American shrub

explanation.surface: A gardener warns that some fruit has been planted right beside a poisonous bush.
explanation.walkthrough: Sumac is a family of shrubs, one species of which (poison sumac) causes rashes like poison ivy.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a small, easy-peeling citrus like a mandarin, so it is a kind of fruit.

clue.text: Benefactor flawlessly working to protect Republican

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: to have something off pat is to know it flawlessly
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A generous donor works tirelessly and perfectly to shield a Republican politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flawlessly' is an odd synonym: it comes from the phrase 'off pat', meaning known perfectly and ready to recite.
explanation.definitionFit: A patron supports an artist or cause with money, which is what a benefactor does.

clue.text: Power goes to the head of local club chairperson

indicators.note: going to the head means taking the front position, so this piece is placed first

blocks.note: P is the symbol for power in physics
a local is someone who lives in the area

explanation.surface: Being made chair of a local club goes to someone's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power goes to the head' reads as the idiom for becoming arrogant; it is really an instruction to put P in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Many clubs and societies call the person who presides over meetings by this title, equivalent to a chair.

clue.text: Couple of leading pieces from this week’s Observer

indicators.note: leading pieces are the ones at the front, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A pair of lead articles from this week's edition of the Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday newspaper, a sister paper of the Guardian; 'leading pieces' sound like lead stories but are initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple is a pair of things, and a pair numbers exactly this many.

clue.text: Old writer given drink finally starts talking

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so this piece is placed last

blocks.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
a pen is a writing implement
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: An elderly author, plied with drink, at last begins to talk freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old writer' looks like a single dead author, but it splits into O and PEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To open up is an idiom for beginning to speak frankly, especially about something previously kept back.

clue.text: Entitled hoo-ha about traditional grub

indicators.note: about can mean moved around, so the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the hyphen

explanation.surface: A privileged person kicks up a fuss about old-fashioned food.
explanation.walkthrough: TOAD IN THE HOLE is a British dish of sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-established British dinner is homely traditional fare, and grub is slang for food.

clue.text: Current prejudices dismissing first hint of affection for bin chickens?

indicators.note: a first hint is the earliest trace, so only the opening letter is taken
dismissing sends something away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
prejudices are biases
the opening letter, which is thrown out

explanation.surface: Modern bigotry has lost any trace of fondness for scavenging birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bin chickens' is Australian slang for the white ibises that raid city rubbish bins; the question mark flags the slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Australians nickname these long-billed wading birds for their habit of scavenging food from rubbish bins.

clue.text: Everything is in place for learning very old language

blocks.note: uni is short for university
V is the abbreviation for very
Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic

explanation.surface: Everything is set up at a school for studying an ancient tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very old language' reads as one phrase, but 'very' gives only V and the language is ERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos comprises all existing matter, space and time, so it is literally all there is.

clue.text: Formal clothing good to have after ironing

indicators.note: after means coming later, so these pieces follow the other

blocks.note: ironing smooths things out, evening them
G is the abbreviation for good
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Smart clothes are best worn freshly pressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ironing' pretends to be the laundry chore; read as making level it is the first word of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A long dress worn to formal occasions at night, so it is a garment of formal wear.

clue.text: Back, bottom, and top of a diamond?

blocks.note: to back a motion is to second it
the bottom of something is its base

explanation.surface: The rear, underside and upper face of a gemstone.
explanation.walkthrough: The diamond is a baseball field, not a jewel; seen from home plate, the bag at the far point is at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball the bases form a diamond, and this one sits at the point opposite home plate, drawn at the top.

clue.text: Disparage one framework supporting study

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting means sitting underneath, so these pieces come below

blocks.note: a den is a private room for study
I is the Roman numeral one
a grate is a framework of metal bars

explanation.surface: A critic runs down a theoretical framework that underpins some research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Framework supporting study' sounds academic, but study is a room and the framework is a fireplace grate.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to criticise unfairly or belittle someone or something's worth.

clue.text: Watch episodes pretty vacuously

indicators.note: vacuously means emptily, so each word is emptied of its middle and only the outer letters stay

blocks.note: the first and last letters
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone watches TV episodes with a blank, empty-headed stare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuously' reads as describing the viewing, but it tells you to empty each of the two words that follow 'Watch'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean to see or catch sight of something, though the answer is more literary.

clue.text: Each phone download carries over

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: an app is software downloaded to a phone
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Every phone app you download brings something over with it.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is a set of six balls in cricket, written O on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means per item, as in tickets costing ten pounds per person.

clue.text: Pressure now on doubles partners, perhaps

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure
a programme now on is being broadcast

explanation.surface: The pressure is now on a doubles team at a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure now on' reads as a sports commentator's phrase; 'now on' is a show on air.
explanation.definitionFit: Two players teamed up for a doubles match form a matched pair, and 'perhaps' marks them as one example.

clue.text: Improper form of online chat

indicators.note: a form of something is a new shape of it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A certain kind of internet chatting is inappropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole two-word phrase 'online chat' is the fodder, with exactly the ten letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unprincipled or morally unsuitable is improper, falling short of accepted standards of conduct.

clue.text: In town, is ignoring every odd character best? Always!

indicators.note: leaving out the first, third, fifth letters and so on keeps only the even-numbered ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
the best is the top

explanation.surface: An exasperated question about whether snubbing the local eccentrics is always wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd character' sounds like a strange person in town; it means the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done without pause or interruption goes on continually, which the exclamation 'Always!' conveys.

clue.text: They don’t like people getting on

definitions.text: They don’t like people getting on

blocks.clueFragment: They don’t like people getting on
blocks.note: surface reading: grumpy bus drivers or passengers who resent people boarding
setter's reading: getting on means growing old, so these are people prejudiced against the elderly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' first suggests boarding a train, or getting along with each other; its third sense is ageing.
explanation.definitionFit: People who discriminate by age, typically against older people, dislike those who are advancing in years.

clue.text: Idiot comedian Seth is a gas!

blocks.note: nit is British slang for a fool
Seth Rogen is a Canadian comic actor

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a foolish comedian is great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is a gas' reads as slang for being hilarious; the gas is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: This colourless element makes up most of the atmosphere, so it is a chemical gas.

clue.text: More wary about guide regularly deserting halfway through

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
halfway through points at the exact middle, so only the central letter is taken

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, Latin for about
the first, third and fifth letters
the fifth of nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone grows more cautious about a guide who keeps abandoning the group midway through tours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deserting' looks like an action of the guide, but it only supplies its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cagey means guarded or secretive, so its comparative describes someone more cautious and noncommittal.

clue.text: Works partly shown on a carousel going round

indicators.note: partly shown means only some of it is visible, so the letters lie within the phrase
going round turns something back on itself, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word, the two short words and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Artworks are exhibited in part on a rotating display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like a verb about a machine; it is a noun for a body of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: The accepted body of an author's writings, or of a genre's key texts, is referred to by this term.

clue.text: Immediate tension as a nut runs wild

indicators.note: running wild means out of control, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tension rises at once when a lunatic goes on the rampage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is part of the letters, not a madman.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening in an instant, without any delay, is immediate.

clue.text: Go on an icy run and nearly lose traction

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a wheel that loses traction slides out of control

explanation.surface: A driver on an icy road almost slides out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: The icy run is a snowy slope, not a frozen road.
explanation.definitionFit: Descending a snow-covered piste on long runners is a way of travelling down a wintry slope.

clue.text: Uncovered fuels catch fire

indicators.note: uncovering strips away the outside, so the first and last letters go

blocks.note: lignite is soft brown coal, burnt as fuel

explanation.surface: Fuel left exposed bursts into flames.
explanation.walkthrough: Lignite is a low-grade brown coal; with its outer letters stripped the plural gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To begin burning is the intransitive sense of the verb, meaning to start to burn.

clue.text: Colour quality of tattoos on chap’s back and head

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken
in an across entry, on means following, so this piece comes after

blocks.note: the final letter
tattoos are informally called ink
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: The vivid shade of the tattoos inked across a man's back and head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' pretends to be a body part; it takes the last letter of chap. Ness appears in British place names for a headland, such as Loch Ness's neighbour Orford Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of being a rosy colour is a quality of that hue, so the noun names a colour quality.
